subtitle: A how-to guide for writing routing policies in the Internet Routing Registry using RPSL.

tldr.problem: Internet service providers need a way to write down and share their routing policies in a standardized format so that networks can coordinate with each other and diagnose routing problems.
tldr.mechanism: RPSL is a language that lets you describe routing policies using database objects that are registered in the Internet Routing Registry. These objects describe how your network peers with others and which routes it will accept or announce.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can publish their policies in a central registry, use tools to generate router configurations automatically, and verify that their peering agreements are consistent. RPSL became the standard way to describe routing policies on the Internet.

facts.label: Replication frequency
facts.value: At least once a day, as often as every 10 minutes

today: RFC 2650 is an Informational document that remains a standard reference for ISPs learning RPSL. RPSL itself was standardized in RFC 2622 and continues to be the primary language for describing routing policies in the Internet Routing Registry.

sections.title: Introduction to RPSL
sections.content:
RFC 2650 is a tutorial on the Routing Policy Specification Language (RPSL), a language for describing how autonomous systems (networks) control the flow of routing information between each other. The RFC explains how to use RPSL to register policies in the Internet Routing Registry (IRR), a set of five databases that hold routing policies and allow networks to coordinate.

The tutorial is aimed at engineers in Internet service providers (ISPs) who already understand routing but are new to RPSL. It explains both the language itself and the practical tools used to apply it, including how to use the RAToolSet to generate router configurations from policies.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide for network engineers on how to write down and share the rules their network uses for deciding which routes to accept from neighbors and which routes to send out.

sections.title: Core RPSL Concepts
sections.content:
RPSL builds on RIPE-181, an earlier language that had limitations in practice. The key building blocks are database objects, each holding a piece of routing policy:

Autonomous System (aut-num) objects describe the import and export policies of an AS -- which routes it accepts from each peer and which routes it announces to each peer. An import clause says what routes to accept; an export clause says what routes to announce. For example, an ISP might import all routes from a transit provider but export only its own customers' routes.

Set objects let you group multiple ASes or routes together with a single name. An as-set groups AS numbers (useful for grouping a provider's customers). A route-set groups address prefixes (useful for specifying which address blocks a customer may announce).

Route objects specify which address prefixes are originated (announced) by each AS, and are linked to the aut-num that originates them.

These objects reference each other, allowing operators to write scalable policies that do not need to be edited when customers or address assignments change.
sections.plainLanguage: RPSL has building blocks: one for saying what routes you import and export, one for grouping your customers together, and one for saying which address blocks you own. You link them together to write policies that stay correct even when things change.

sections.title: Writing Peering Policies
sections.content:
A simple peering policy might look like this: import all routes from a transit provider (which provides full Internet routing), but only import routes that originate from a customer's own AS. An ISP announces only its own customers' routes to its transit provider, but announces everything to its customers.

RPSL allows regex-style matching of AS paths (the sequence of ASes a route has traversed). The syntax <^AS3+$> matches routes that originate in AS3 and have gone through only AS3. This prevents accepting routes that have been prepended or altered.

Interface-level peering lets you specify policies for particular physical connections, not just whole autonomous systems. You can also use actions to set BGP attributes like local preference and multi-exit discriminator (MED), which influence route selection at each router.

The RFC walks through increasingly complex examples: simple peering, handling multiple customers, filtering by address space, using sets to avoid editing multiple lines when customers change, and using BGP community attributes to let customers influence the provider's routing decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: You write rules like 'take everything from the big provider' or 'only take routes that came from my customer.' As your network grows, you use groups instead of writing the same rule over and over.

sections.title: Tools for Managing Policies
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main tools in the RAToolSet:

The aut-num object editor (aoe) is a graphical interface for viewing, editing and submitting aut-num objects. It makes it easier to work with policies than editing plain text files.

RtConfig is a tool that takes RPSL policies registered in the IRR and a template source file, and generates vendor-specific router configurations for Cisco, gated, or RSd. A network engineer writes @RtConfig commands in a template file (such as @RtConfig import AS3582 198.32.162.1 AS3701 198.32.162.2), and RtConfig replaces these with actual access lists and route maps that reflect the policies in the IRR. This allows networks to keep policies and configurations synchronized without hand-editing every router.

The RFC also mentions the route object editor (roe) for managing which prefixes each AS originates, and peval, a low-level tool for evaluating policies and extracting data from the registry.
sections.plainLanguage: There are programs that read your policies from the registry and automatically write the real router configuration files, so you do not have to hand-edit them.

sections.title: The Internet Routing Registry
sections.content:
The IRR consists of five databases run independently but synchronized at least once a day (and as often as every 10 minutes). The CA*Net registry in Canada and the CW and ANS registries in the US are private, holding policies only from their members. The RADB and RIPE registries are public and open to any ISP.

Objects are submitted to the registry by email, followed by authentication (such as a password or digital signature). The registry robot processes submissions and notifies the submitter of success or errors. Best practice is to register in only one registry to avoid inconsistencies; the five registries then replicate your data.

Networks query the registry using whois, and tools like RtConfig can read policies to generate configurations. Registered policies can be analyzed for consistency, compared to real-world peerings, and used to diagnose routing problems.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five shared notebooks (registries) where networks store their policies. You put your policies in one, and the others copy them. Tools can then read these to check if your real routers match what you said they would do.
